Lawmakers in Italy are paving the way to again have nuclear power as part of the country’s energy mix. Legislators in Italy’s Senate in September approved a measure that supports Premier Giorgia Meloni’s drive to meet climate goals and bolster energy security. Officials have acknowledged that construction of new reactors is likely still several years away, but said the bill is important because it establishes a legal framework to pursue next-generation nuclear technologies. The legislation authorizes the government to draft implementing decrees over the next year that would look at safety standards and licensing of new reactors, and provide guidance for waste management. It also would set the criteria needed to choose the sites of new nuclear power plants.
A public referendum 1987 led Italy to move away from nuclear power following the 1986 Chernobyl disaster. The country closed its last nuclear power stations in 1990. Government officials in 2008 said they wanted to revive nuclear power, and then-Minister of Economic Development Claudio Scajola made a proposal to build up to 10 new reactors by 2030. That plan met opposition after the 2011 Fukushima incident in Japan, and voters in Italy later that year overwhelmingly said they supported a ban on nuclear construction.
Meloni’s government, though, has revived the discussion around nuclear power, with a particular focus on small modular reactors (SMRs). Gilberto Pichetto Fratin, the country’s minister of the Environment and Energy Security, after the September approval said, “Today, Italy is taking a step toward the future: the approval of the government’s mandate for new, sustainable nuclear power completes a process begun three years ago, aimed at exploring the potential of this new, clean, and sustainable technology. Nuclear power is not a return to the past: it is a winning technology, which, when integrated with renewables, can deliver extraordinary results for our energy security, toward neutrality by 2050.”
U.S. officials also are talking with counterparts in Italy about the country’s restart of nuclear power. Vannia Gava, Italy’s deputy minister for Environment and Energy Security, met recently with Jarrod Agen, executive director of the White House National Energy Dominance Council, during an official visit to Washington, D.C. “With Jarrod Agen, we shared at the White House a perspective that unites Italy and the United States: energy security is national security,” Gava said. “For manufacturing countries like Italy and the United States, this means ensuring reliable energy at affordable costs for businesses, diversifying sources, including next-generation nuclear power in the energy mix, and choosing stable and reliable partners.”
Nuward, a French company and a subsidiary of multinational energy company EDF, plus Edison and Italian industrial partners Ansaldo and Maire, earlier this year stressed their “common vision for the development of small modular reactors (SMRs) in Europe and their ambition to deploy a first reactor in Italy by 2035.” Newcleo, a France-headquartered developer of lead-cooled advanced modular reactors, also has considerable operations in Italy, including the first non-nuclear precursor prototype of its lead-cooled fast reactor. Last year it signed a memorandum of understanding with Italian cement association Federbeton to assess the potential for Newcleo’s technologies to work with the cement industry. Nuward recently said it wants to have a fleet of 10 of its SMRs across five European Union (EU) member countries, with initial construction beginning in 2030. Nuward in a statement posted on social media wrote, “Beyond the deployment of a first reactor, this momentum creates tangible opportunities for Italian industry to contribute to the development of the technology and become part of the value chain of the future European #SMR programme.”
1. This is a conceptual rendering that illustrates the integration of Terra Innovatum’s SOLO Micro-Modular Nuclear Reactor into an industrial complex, where it would provide electricity and thermal energy through cogeneration. Courtesy: Terra Innovatum Global N.V
Italy-headquartered Terra Innovatum Global N.V. , which has developed the SOLO Micro-Modular Reactor (Figure 1), is among the groups that support the country’s return to nuclear power. “Today represents an important milestone for Italy and for the broader European nuclear industry,” said Alessandro Petruzzi, co-founder and CEO of Terra Innovatum, after the move by the country’s lawmakers in September. “Italy has remained an important contributor to the nuclear supply chains of both Europe and the United States, with extraordinary capabilities across nuclear engineering, advanced manufacturing, and energy infrastructure. The decision to create a pathway for the return of nuclear energy recognizes the increasingly important role advanced nuclear technologies can play in providing reliable, carbon-free power.”
Terra Innovatum made a presentation about its SOLO technology during the 70th International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) General Conference in Vienna, Austria, in September. Company officials have said they think smaller, modular, factory-manufactured reactors such as SOLO can expand nuclear energy beyond traditional large-scale power plants. Terra Innovatum is developing the SOLO micro-modular reactor around proven nuclear technologies. It would use low-enriched uranium fuel.
“As Italy advances its new nuclear framework, the distinction between technologies in R&D [research and development] and those approaching commercial deployment will become increasingly important,” said Giordano Morichi, founding partner and managing director of Global Business Development and Investor Relations for Terra Innovatum. “SOLO was engineered for commercialization, with approximately $4 billion in pre-commercial commitments across data centers, industrial projects, and other energy-intensive applications globally.”
Dr. Massimo Morichi, Chief Strategy Officer (CSO) for Terra Innovatum, told POWER that the government’s decision “reflects a reassessment of Italy’s long-term energy needs rather than a single political or technological breakthrough. Meloni has presented nuclear power as a means of strengthening national energy security, while Fratin has argued that it could contribute to a more balanced and competitive energy mix. The government’s longer-term ambition is to integrate nuclear generation into Italy’s decarbonization strategy.”
The CSO said there is also a “significant industrial dimension. Italy retains nuclear engineering, manufacturing, research, and decommissioning capabilities despite having no operating commercial nuclear power plants. Building on this established expertise, a new program could create further opportunities for domestic suppliers, engineering companies, and research institutions, while strengthening Italy’s positioning as a key industrial player in the international market for advanced reactors. The timing is very significant because nuclear technologies are evolving, European countries are reconsidering their energy strategies, and modular reactor designs are attracting renewed investment. Italy is seeking to establish a framework now so that it can participate in this emerging market rather than remain dependent on technologies developed elsewhere.”
Terra Innovatum is advancing SOLO through the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission licensing process. The company, pending regulatory approvals, is targeting first-of-its-kind deployment next year, with commercial deployment and scale-up by the end of 2028.
Morichi said, “Italy must also distinguish between the cost of building a reactor and the cost of the electricity it produces over its lifetime. A smaller project may require less capital overall but can have a higher cost per megawatt than a successfully delivered large plant. The promised economic advantages therefore depend on execution and repeat deployment, not just reactor size. For Italy, the attraction is not simply to build smaller reactors, it is to establish a repeatable model that could support a broader nuclear program while limiting the financial and construction risks associated with each individual project.”
Gava at the meeting with Agen said the U.S. and Italy also have talked about addressing vulnerabilities in supply chains for the energy sector, in addition to collaborating on nuclear power. “During our discussion, we focused on critical raw materials, on which energy security will increasingly depend in the coming years, and whose refining is currently concentrated in very few countries,” said Gava. “This is a vulnerability that the West must address together, building shared supply chains and partnerships with producing countries.”
Gava highlighted Italy’s critical minerals agreement with the U.S., noting it could strengthen the Italian government’s role in the Pax Silica initiative, a U.S.-led project launched in December of last year. Officials said the strategy is designed to build a resilient, allied economic consensus around artificial intelligence, semiconductors, and critical mineral supply chains. The EU already has selected five Italy-led projects focused on critical materials processing and recycling.
—Darrell Proctor is a senior editor for POWER.
